title: Racing
intro: Motor racing is the business of getting a car round a track, or from one point to another, in less time than anyone else. The same physics governs a race car on a real circuit and a car in a driving simulator or racing video game: four small patches of rubber, each about the size of a hand, have to do all the braking, turning and accelerating. This topic explains that physics, the techniques drivers use to exploit it, how cars are set up and tuned, and the rules and tactics of wheel-to-wheel racing. Everything here applies both on a real track and in a game; where the two differ, the pages say so.

blocks.text: A lap is a sequence of straights joined by corners. On the straights the car is limited by its engine power and its aerodynamic drag. In the corners, and in the braking zones before them, it is limited by grip: the most force the tyres can make before they slide. Most of the time a driver can win or lose is in the braking zones and corners, because that is where the car is on the limit and where the driver's choices change what happens.

items: Grip. The tyres make every force the car feels. How much they can make depends on the tyre compound, its temperature and pressure, the road surface, the load pressing the tyre down, and any downforce from the wings and floor. See #/games/racing/vehicle-dynamics.

The line. The path the car takes through a corner sets how tight the turn is, and so how fast it can be taken, and how early the driver can accelerate onto the next straight. See #/games/racing/racing-line.

Technique. How the driver uses the brake, throttle and steering: braking as late and as hard as the tyres allow, carrying the right speed to the apex, and getting back to full throttle as early as possible. See #/games/racing/driving-technique.

Setup. How the car is adjusted (tyre pressures, suspension, wings, gearing, differential) changes its balance, which is how it shares grip between the front and rear tyres. See #/games/racing/car-setup.
Racecraft and strategy. In a race, other cars are on the track. Overtaking, defending, tyre and fuel management and pit stops decide results as much as raw pace. See #/games/racing/racecraft.
Practice and data. Drivers improve by measuring: lap times by sector, telemetry traces, and comparison with a faster lap. See #/games/racing/practice-and-data.
Circuit racing: many cars on a closed track for a set number of laps or a set time. Most racing, real and virtual, is this kind.

Open-wheel (single-seater) racing: light cars with exposed wheels and large wings, such as Formula 1, IndyCar and junior formula series. Very high downforce and very sensitive to the air disturbed by a car in front.

Touring car and GT (grand touring) racing: cars based on road-going models, from modified saloons to purpose-built GT3 race cars. GT classes are often equalised by a balance of performance, which adds weight or reduces power on the faster models.

Sports prototypes and endurance racing: closed-cockpit cars built only for racing, in races of 6, 12 or 24 hours with several drivers sharing one car. Endurance racing rewards consistency, fuel and tyre economy, and avoiding damage in traffic of several classes at once.
Rally: one car at a time on closed public roads (tarmac, gravel, snow), timed from point to point, with a co-driver reading pace notes that describe the road ahead.
Drag racing: two cars side by side over a straight quarter mile (402 m) or eighth mile. Everything is launch, traction and reaction time.
Drifting: judged, not timed. Drivers are scored on angle, speed, line and style while the car slides sideways on purpose.
Karting: small open karts with no suspension and no differential. Where almost every racing driver starts, because it teaches the line, braking and racecraft cheaply.

blocks.text: Racing games range from arcade games, which bend physics to be fun and forgiving, to simulators, which model tyre forces, suspension movement, weight transfer and aerodynamics closely enough that real racing teams use them for training. The more realistic the game, the more of this topic carries over unchanged. The main differences are what the driver can feel and what a mistake costs.

items: Feel. A real driver feels the car through the seat, the steering wheel and their inner ear: the onset of a slide arrives as a change in lateral acceleration before it can be seen. A sim driver has only the picture, the sound and the force feedback in the wheel (and sometimes a motion rig), so they learn to read the car through the steering weight, the tyre noise and how the view rotates.

Cost of a mistake. In a game a crash costs a reset or a lost race; on a real track it costs money and can cost injury. Real drivers build up to the limit more gradually, and leave more margin where the run-off is a wall.

Repeatability. A simulator gives the same track conditions lap after lap, which makes it ideal for learning a track, testing setups and practising specific corners. Real conditions change: track temperature, rubber laid on the surface, wind and wear.

Assists. Games often offer driving aids: anti-lock brakes, traction control, stability control, automatic gears and a drawn-on racing line. Many real race cars have ABS and traction control too; stability control and line guides are mainly a game feature. See #/games/racing/practice-and-data.

blocks.text: A useful habit for any racing question: ask what each tyre is being asked to do at that moment, and whether it has any grip left to give. Almost every handling problem, setup change and driving technique comes back to that.
